provenance.other: “the mighty hunter” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 10:9, where the epithet is given twice in the one sentence: 'He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.' The Book of Mormon supplies the name and the epithet in the same breath — 'the name of the valley was Nimrod, being called after the mighty hunter' — and its parenthesis is a gloss on Genesis, not a fact about a valley.
provenance.significance: Two things the gloss does not say. First, the KJV's epithet is not 'mighty hunter' but 'mighty hunter BEFORE THE LORD', and the valley named for a man defined by his standing before the LORD is where, three verses later, the Lord comes down and stands in a cloud and talks with the brother of Jared. The Jaredites keep the appointment Nimrod's title advertises. Second, Genesis 10:10 makes Babel the beginning of Nimrod's kingdom, and the book this chapter opens is the book of a people leaving Babel: Ether 1 is built on Genesis 11:1-9 and the confounding of the language. So the departure from Babel is staged in the valley of the man who founded it. The etymological parenthesis is doing narrative work — it tells a reader who knows Genesis 10-11 that the Jaredites are not merely leaving a city but walking out of a genealogy.

2:1.note: The chapter's opening parenthesis is a footnote to Genesis 10. 'Mighty hunter' is a KJV singleton and is not an ordinary description of a man; it is Nimrod's formal title, and the Book of Mormon attaches it to the name Nimrod exactly as Genesis does. Dependence is not seriously deniable and the row is 'certain' on that ground, though the borrowing is three words and stands far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold — it is one of his passages in no sense. What makes it more than an etymology is placement: it is the first of a run of Genesis 6-11 contacts that carries the whole chapter, and the valley it names is where the theophany of 2:4-5 happens.
2:1.text: He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.

provenance.other: “to keep seed alive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 7:3, and the fuller “seed alive upon the face” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one: 'Of fowls also of the air by sevens, the male and the female; to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth.' “male and female” occurs in 7 KJV verses, of which Genesis 6:19 and 7:16 are the ark's; “of every sort” occurs in 5, of which Genesis 6:19, 6:20 and 7:14 are the ark's.
provenance.significance: Read the three verses 2:1-3 as one inventory and it is the ark's manifest, item for item and in Genesis's own order: flocks male and female of every kind (Genesis 6:19-20), fowls (7:3), food to be gathered and carried (6:21), and seed for the face of the land (7:3). What Genesis withholds it withholds here too — the Jaredites are not told they are re-enacting the flood, and the text never says so. But the deseret, the swarms of bees, the fish carried alive in a vessel of water are a solution to a problem only an ark has: how a whole biosphere crosses a great water. The chapter will make that explicit at 2:17 and 2:20, where the barges acquire the ark's door and the ark's window. Here the argument is still made only by the packing list.

2:3.note: The machine proposed nothing at 2:1 or 2:3 and Job 12:7 at 2:2 on 'fowls of the air', which occurs in 13 KJV verses and points nowhere. Read the three verses together, however, and the shared item is not a phrase but a schedule — breeding pairs of livestock, fowls, and seed for replanting a land — which in the KJV exists in exactly one place. The clinching detail is the last one: 'all manner of that which was upon the face of the land, seeds of every kind' against Genesis 7:3's 'to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth', a KJV singleton that supplies both the seed and the face. The row is 'high' rather than 'certain' because no clause is reproduced; it is an argument about an inventory, and a reader could hold that any migrating people would pack this way. Against that: Genesis is the only text that describes packing this way, and the destination is across a sea in a sealed vessel.
2:3.text: Of fowls also of the air by sevens, the male and the female; to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth.

provenance.route: Numbers 11:25 / Exodus 33:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “came down in a cloud” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 11:25. “talked with Moses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 33:9, where the cloudy pillar descends and stands at the door of the tabernacle. Numbers 12:5 supplies the third element the Book of Mormon has and neither of the other two does — the Lord comes down in the cloud and STANDS: 'And the LORD came down in the pillar of the cloud, and stood in the door of the tabernacle.' Ether 2:5 has 'as he stood in a cloud'.
provenance.significance: The cloud in the KJV does two different jobs and the Book of Mormon takes both. In Exodus 13 it leads a nation; in Exodus 33-34 and Numbers 11-12 it is what a single man speaks to God through, and specifically it is the medium of a conversation the man is not permitted to see through — 'thou canst not see my face' (Exodus 33:20). Ether 2:4's clause 'and he was in a cloud, and the brother of Jared saw him not' states the Mosaic condition exactly, and states it in a chapter whose whole business is that the brother of Jared will, in the next chapter, see. The cloud is put in place at 2:4 so that Ether 3 can take it away.
provenance.alternative: Exodus 34:5's 'And the LORD descended in the cloud, and stood with him there' is also a KJV singleton for 'descended in the cloud' and holds the descent and the standing in one verse; it is offered here as composite rather than as the source because the Book of Mormon's verb is 'came down', which is Numbers 11:25's and 12:5's, not 'descended'.

2:4.note: Four words, but they are the four rarest available: 'came down in a cloud' is a KJV singleton and the Book of Mormon has the elements distributed across 2:4 and 2:5 — came down, in a cloud, talked with, stood. No one of the three candidate verses holds all four, which is why the row carries composites rather than claiming a single source; what is not in doubt is that the theophany is built out of the Sinai-and-tabernacle cloud and not out of anything else in the KJV. The machine's top candidate here was Judges 14:7, five words of Samson going down to talk with a woman at Timnath, which is filed in the exclusion register.
2:4.text: And the LORD came down in a cloud, and spake unto him, and took of the spirit that was upon him, and gave it unto the seventy elders: and it came to pass, that, when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied, and did not cease.

provenance.other: Deuteronomy 1:33 reads: 'Who went in the way before you, to search you out a place to pitch your tents in, in fire by night, to shew you by what way ye should go, and in a cloud by day.' “went before them by day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 13:21; “wherein they should go” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Nehemiah 9:12 and 9:19, both retellings of it. Deuteronomy 1:33 is the only one of the three that holds the going-before, the showing of the way, the cloud AND the pitching of tents, and Ether has all four across 2:5 and 2:13.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 1:33 is Moses reminding a generation that the guidance they are about to refuse was itemised. Ether 2:5 gives the itemisation and then, at 2:14, the refusal: four years camped at Moriancumer without calling on the name of the Lord, and a three-hour chastening for it. The Jaredite journey is set up as the wilderness journey and then permitted to fail in the wilderness journey's characteristic way — not by rebellion but by forgetting the one who is going before. That the guidance is 'continual' at 2:6 ('being directed continually by the hand of the Lord') makes the four silent years at 2:13 the more pointed.

2:5.note: 'The Lord did go before them, and did talk with them as he stood in a cloud, and gave directions whither they should travel.' Every clause has a KJV counterpart in the wilderness-guidance formula, and 'gave directions whither they should travel' is the KJV's 'to shew you by what way ye should go' in other words. Two verses later the same source supplies 'they pitched their tents' at 2:13. The row is 'high' and not 'certain' because none of the three candidate verses is reproduced clause for clause; the Book of Mormon paraphrases a formula rather than quoting a verse. Note that Deuteronomy 1:33's guidance is 'in fire by night', which the Lord will explicitly withhold from the Jaredites at 2:23 — see the Exodus 13:21 row there.
2:5.text: Who went in the way before you, to search you out a place to pitch your tents in, in fire by night, to shew you by what way ye should go, and in a cloud by day.

provenance.other: “land of promise” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:9: 'By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise.' The Old Testament never uses the phrase; it says 'the land which the LORD sware unto thy fathers to give thee'. Every 'land of promise' in the Book of Mormon is therefore an English phrase available only from the New Testament.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:9's promised land comes with two qualifications the Book of Mormon keeps and one it inverts. Kept: the promise is held by sojourners who dwell in tents — and Ether 2:13 has the Jaredites dwelling in tents on the seashore for four years before they ever reach it. Inverted: in Hebrews the land is entered 'as in a strange country' and the patriarchs never possess it, whereas Ether 2:7-12 turns the land into a possession governed by a standing condition. The reader who recovers Hebrews 11 finds that the chapter's whole point is that the promise was NOT received (11:13, 11:39), which is a strange foundation for a decree about who shall possess a continent — and a very apt one for a book whose land of promise is twice depopulated.

2:7.note: A three-word phrase, but a KJV singleton, and a phrase the Book of Mormon uses as a technical term from 1 Nephi onward. The row is written here rather than passed over as an internal formula because Ether is a new book in a different hand — Moroni abridging a record that predates Lehi — and ADJUDICATING §4's ruling is that a phrase re-entering across a book boundary gets its link; the argument for the source was made at 1 Nephi 2:20 and is not restated. What is new here is the use: 1 Nephi applies the phrase to a journey, Ether 2:7-12 makes it the subject of a legal decree.
2:7.text: By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:

provenance.route: Psalm 95:11 → Hebrews 4:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “sworn in my wrath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 4:3. The same oath appears twice more and both times in the other form: Psalm 95:11 'Unto whom I sware in my wrath', and Hebrews 3:11 'So I sware in my wrath'. “sworn in his wrath” occurs in 0 KJV verses — the third-person is the Book of Mormon's own adjustment to reported speech.
provenance.significance: The oath in Psalm 95 and in Hebrews 3-4 is an oath of EXCLUSION: God swears that a generation shall not enter his rest, and the whole argument of Hebrews 3-4 hangs on the threat's still being open. Ether 2:8 swears in the same words about entry to a land, and then does something the source does not: it makes the oath conditional and perpetual rather than retrospective, so that the sentence passed on the wilderness generation becomes a standing charter for every nation that possesses this land. Recover the context and the 'righteous people' for whom the land is preserved at 2:7 are standing where the carcases fell in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:17).
provenance.alternative: mediation-check.py run on this verse returns divergences pointing both ways: it scores 'should not' for Psalm 95:11. That point is an artifact and should not be read as evidence — Ether 2:8's 'should' belongs to 'whoso should possess' and 'should serve him', not to entering a rest, and the verse has no rest-clause at all. The one clause genuinely shared is the oath formula, and there the tool's other decisive point stands: the Book of Mormon has 'sworn', which in the KJV is Hebrews 4:3's word alone.

2:8.note: A four-word contact carrying a real mediation finding. The KJV renders one Hebrew oath three times, twice as 'sware' and once, at Hebrews 4:3, as 'sworn'; the Book of Mormon has 'sworn'. That is the whole of the argument and it is decisive in the way CONVENTIONS §7 asks for — a single word settling which English form was in front of the writer, as 'ruler' not 'prince' does at 1 Nephi 22:20. It also separates this row from the book's other uses of the oath: Alma 12:35 and Jacob 1:7 quote the rest-clause and cannot settle their own mediation, whereas Ether 2:8 quotes only the oath and settles it outright. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his passages.
2:8.text: For we which have believed do enter into rest, as he said, As I have sworn in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest: although the works were finished from the foundation of the world.

provenance.other: “iniquity of the Amorites” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 15:16: 'But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.' “not yet full” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Genesis 15:16 and John 7:8. The KJV has no phrase 'fulness of iniquity'; what it has is this single idea, that a people's iniquity has a measure and that dispossession waits on the measure being filled.
provenance.significance: Genesis 15:16 is the verse that reconciles the promise of Canaan with the four hundred years before it is kept: the land is not empty, and the sitting tenants are not yet guilty enough to lose it. Ether 2:9-10 takes that single explanatory clause and makes it the constitution of a hemisphere — 'it is not until the fulness of iniquity among the children of the land, that they are swept off' — and then, at 2:11, turns it on the reader: 'this cometh unto you, O ye Gentiles … that ye may not bring down the fulness of the wrath of God upon you, as the inhabitants of the land hath hitherto done.' The Gentiles are addressed in the position of the Amorites. That is the metalepsis: a verse written to justify a conquest is quoted to warn the conquerors.

2:10.note: No clause is reproduced; the contact is a doctrine and its distinctive measure-metaphor, which in the KJV belongs to one verse. The row is 'moderate' because 'fulness of iniquity' is not a KJV phrase and a reader could locate the idea instead in the harvest-of-wrath imagery of Joel 3:13 and Revelation 14 — which Ether 2:15 does in fact reach for, in the same speech, with 'fully ripe'. The two are not rivals so much as the two halves of one figure, and I have adjudicated each where its own wording sits. The 1830's plural 'the everlasting decrees of God', singular in 1920, is worth noting: the first edition treats this as a body of law rather than a single ruling, which is what a charter built out of Genesis 15:16 would be.
2:10.whyNot: The verbal contact is one word ('full'/'fulness') plus a shared metaphor, which is thin enough that a cautious editor would decline it. What holds the row up is context rather than volume: Ether 2:9-11 states, three times in three verses, the exact proposition Genesis 15:16 exists to state, and states it about a land whose inhabitants are to be dispossessed by incomers.
2:10.text: But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.

provenance.other: “strive with man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:3: 'And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.' The Book of Mormon has 'my spirit will not always strive with man' — seven words in the KJV's order with 'shall' modernised to 'will'. The 1830 reads lower-case 'my spirit', as the KJV does; 1920 capitalised it to 'my Spirit', which quietly converts a KJV clause into a doctrinal term.
provenance.significance: This is where the chapter's Genesis substructure becomes impossible to miss, because the Lord answers a repentance with the sentence that introduces the Flood. Genesis 6:3 is the verdict; Genesis 6:14-16 is the ark; Genesis 7:16 is the door shut. Ether 2:15 is the verdict, 2:17 is the sealed vessel, 2:17 again is the door shut — in Genesis's order, one verse after another. And the verdict is repurposed: in Genesis the striving ends and the world is drowned, whereas here the same sentence is spoken to the man who is about to be preserved through water, as a condition on his continuing. The brother of Jared is told, in the words that condemned Noah's generation, that he is not yet of that generation.

2:15.note: Seven words verbatim from a KJV singleton, and the only serious question is whether it is a fresh borrowing or the Book of Mormon reusing its own formula — the clause has already appeared at 1 Nephi 7:14, 2 Nephi 26:11 and Mormon 5:16. ADJUDICATING §4's ruling that a phrase re-entering in a different hand gets its link would be enough on its own, but there is a stronger reason to write it here: at the other three occurrences the clause is cited as a general principle about the withdrawal of the Spirit, and here alone it stands in its own Genesis setting, four verses ahead of an ark. This is the one place in the Book of Mormon where Genesis 6:3 is quoted with Genesis 6-8 around it. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages.
2:15.text: And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.

provenance.route: Jeremiah 26:19 / 2 Samuel 24:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon (1830 only)
provenance.other: “repented him of the evil” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses — 2 Samuel 24:16, 1 Chronicles 21:15 and Jeremiah 26:19 — and the subject is God in all three. Jeremiah 26:19 is the closest, adding the relative clause the Book of Mormon also has: 'the LORD repented him of the evil which he had pronounced against them' against Ether 2:15's 'repented him of the evil which he had done', a run of six words. The 1830 reads 'repented him of the evil'; 1920 deleted the reflexive pronoun and the modern text reads 'repented of the evil', which is not a KJV construction at all.
provenance.significance: The KJV reserves this reflexive idiom for God relenting of a punishment he had determined — the angel over Jerusalem, the sentence on Micah's Jerusalem — and never uses it of a man repenting of his own sin. Ether 2:15 puts a man in the construction, and does it in the sentence immediately before the Lord says 'I will forgive thee'. Whether that is a solecism or a deliberate reversal cannot be settled from the text; what can be settled is that the KJV's grammar of divine relenting has been transferred to human repentance, and that the transfer is legible only in the first edition.

2:15.note: A six-word run in a construction the KJV uses three times, all of God. This is a CONVENTIONS §8 row before it is anything else: the borrowing exists in the 1830 and has been edited out of the text most readers have, so the modern 'repented of the evil which he had done' shows no contact with Jeremiah 26:19 at all while the running text of this catalogue shows six words of it. Confidence is 'moderate' rather than higher because the idiom could have been picked up from the KJV's general register rather than from any one of the three verses, and because the sense is genuinely different — God relenting of a judgment is not a man being sorry for a sin.
2:15.whyNot: If 'repented him' was simply archaic English available to the writer independently of any verse, then the run proves only the register and not a source, and the row should be read as evidence of KJV idiom rather than of Jeremiah 26. Note also that the machine ranked this the chapter's strongest candidate (rarity 2.37) partly because 'which he had' is filler; strip it and the distinctive contact is four words.
2:15.text: Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him at all to death? did he not fear the LORD, and besought the LORD, and the LORD repented him of the evil which he had pronounced against them? Thus might we procure great evil against our souls.

provenance.other: “fully ripe” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:18: 'Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe.' Joel 3:13, which Revelation is rewriting, has 'put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe' — 'ripe', not 'fully ripe'. The Book of Mormon has the intensified form.
provenance.significance: The vintage of Revelation 14:18-20 ends in a winepress trodden outside the city until blood comes out to the horses' bridles; it is the KJV's most violent image of a judgment that waits on ripeness. Ether 2:15 applies it to a single man's continuing in sin. That compression — an apocalyptic harvest of the nations used as a warning to one repentant person — is what the figure does here, and it ties the private rebuke at Moriancumer back to the public decree of 2:9-10, where the same ripeness governs whether a nation is swept off. The Lord's answer to the brother of Jared restates the land's charter in the second person.

2:15.note: Two words, but a KJV singleton and the exact point where Revelation intensifies its Old Testament source: 'ripe' is Joel's, 'fully ripe' is John's. The Book of Mormon takes John's form and applies it to a person rather than to the vine of the earth, and it does so in a chapter that has already twice used ripeness as the trigger for dispossession (2:9, 2:10). Confidence is 'moderate' because a two-word contact cannot carry more on its own, and because the metaphor of ripened iniquity is common enough in the Book of Mormon's own idiom that this could be its formula rather than a fresh borrowing — the reason for writing the row anyway is that the formula's distinctive word is available from exactly one KJV verse.
2:15.text: And another angel came out from the altar, which had power over fire; and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe.

provenance.other: “shut him in” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 7:16: 'And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in.' “pitch it within and without” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:14, which is the ark's watertightness and the KJV's only instruction to seal a vessel. “the door of the ark” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:16. The Book of Mormon's own “the door thereof” occurs in 0 KJV verses, but 'the side thereof' at Genesis 6:16 and the enumerated 'the top thereof, and the sides thereof' of the tabernacle furniture at Exodus 30:3 are the register it is written in.
provenance.significance: Genesis gives the ark three specifications and Ether 2:17-20 works through all three, changing each. Genesis 6:14 pitches it within and without; Ether makes it 'exceeding tight … that they would hold water like unto a dish', which is the same requirement stated as a test rather than a material. Genesis 6:16 sets the door in the side; Ether puts the door in the enumeration with the top, the bottom and the ends, because a vessel that will be submerged has no side that is not a bottom. And Genesis 7:16 has the LORD shut Noah in from outside — the ark's most theologically loaded sentence, since it means Noah could not have opened it — whereas Ether 2:17's door is shut by the Jaredites and 2:20's air-hole is unstopped by them at need. The Jaredites are sealed in a vessel they can open. That difference is the pivot of the whole episode: they are not passengers but petitioners, which is why the next question they ask gets answered by being handed back.

2:17.note: No clause is reproduced and the row rests on a construction sequence rather than on wording: seal the vessel, specify the door, shut the door. What makes it more than a general resemblance is that the KJV describes the sealing of a vessel exactly once and the shutting of its door exactly once, both in Genesis 6-7, and that Ether 2:15 has just quoted Genesis 6:3 verbatim two verses earlier. The 1830 is materially better evidence than the modern text here and at 2:20: it enumerates 'the bottom thereof … the sides thereof … the ends thereof … the top thereof … the length thereof … the door thereof', and at 2:20 'a hole in the top thereof, and also in the bottom thereof … unstop the hole thereof … stop the hole thereof', four of which 1920 deleted outright. The KJV's construction idiom — Genesis 6:16's 'the side thereof', Exodus 30:2-3's 'the length thereof … the top thereof, and the sides thereof … the horns thereof' — is thickest in the first edition and has been thinned in the one readers use.
2:17.text: And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in.

provenance.other: “I have performed” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, 1 Samuel 15:13 and Romans 15:28; only the first is a report of obedience made in the Lord's name, and it shares five consecutive words with Ether 2:18 ('Lord, I have performed the'). The composite Deuteronomy 26:13 is the KJV's other avowal-of-compliance formula — 'I have done according to all that thou hast commanded me' — and supplies the Book of Mormon's second clause, 'the work which thou hast commanded me'.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 15:13 is the KJV's most famous false report. Saul greets Samuel with 'I have performed the commandment of the LORD' and is answered with 'What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears?'; the chapter ends with the kingdom torn from him. Ether 2:18's report is true, and is answered not with an accusation but with the discovery that the obedience was not sufficient — the barges are built exactly as commanded and they are dark and airless. Read against Saul, the interest of the verse is that doing what you were told turns out not to be the end of the matter, which is precisely the lesson Ether 3 will draw out when the Lord refuses to solve the light problem himself.
provenance.alternative: The formula may be the KJV's general idiom of compliance rather than 1 Samuel 15:13 specifically; Deuteronomy 26:13's tithe avowal is the same speech-act without the irony, and is recorded as composite for that reason.

2:18.note: A five-word run on a two-verse KJV rarity, and the machine's top candidate for the verse. What keeps it at 'moderate' is that 'I have performed the work which thou hast commanded me' is exactly the sentence anyone writing in KJV English would produce for this situation, and the shared context is only the speech-act. What argues for it is that the KJV supplies the speech-act once and once only in these words, and that the Book of Mormon is elsewhere alert to the Saul narrative.
2:18.whyNot: The senses of the two reports are opposed — Saul is lying and the brother of Jared is not — and this catalogue's own exclusion register is full of entries declining links on exactly that ground. The row is written rather than excluded because the opposition is between the reports' truth-values and not between their meanings: both are a servant telling God the assignment is complete, which is the rarest thing about either verse.
2:18.text: And Samuel came to Saul: and Saul said unto him, Blessed be thou of the LORD: I have performed the commandment of the LORD.

provenance.other: “no light in them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 8:20: 'To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.' The Book of Mormon reproduces six words, 'there is no light in them', and has the same clause in a different order at 2:19 ('in them there is no light'). The clause has already been transcribed at 2 Nephi 18:20 as part of the Isaiah block, so its English was in the record before Moroni abridged Ether.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's darkness is the darkness of consulting the dead instead of the law; the sentence is a judgment on necromancers, and the light that is absent is doctrinal. Ether 2:22 uses the identical clause for the plain fact that sixteen sealed wooden hulls have no windows. That is metalepsis running the other way from the usual: the source's figurative meaning is drained off and its literal one restored. The gain is not in Ether 2 but in Ether 3, where the literal problem is solved by the Lord touching sixteen stones and the man who asked for light sees the finger of God — so the chapter that borrows Isaiah's phrase for want of daylight ends with the most direct revelation in the book. The recovered context supplies the frame: 'to the law and to the testimony' is Isaiah's instruction to consult God rather than the dead, and consulting God directly is exactly what the brother of Jared does.

2:22.note: Six consecutive words on a KJV singleton, which by the standard of the 1 Nephi 1:14 row is enough to catalogue as a quotation on volume alone; it is kept at 'allusion' because the clause is a natural English sentence for the situation and the writer need not have felt he was citing Isaiah. Rarity settles the source regardless — the KJV says 'no light in them' once. The link is adjudicated here rather than at 2:19, where the same words appear in the inverted order, because 2:22 has the KJV's own word order; 2:19 is cross-referenced in the exclusion register.
2:22.text: To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.

provenance.other: “a window shalt thou make” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:16: 'A window shalt thou make to the ark, and in a cubit shalt thou finish it above; and the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof.' The Book of Mormon does not quote it. It denies it: 'ye cannot have windows, for they will be dashed in pieces.' Genesis 8:6 is the window's only other appearance, when Noah opens it to release the raven.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's sharpest gesture and it is made by subtraction. The KJV's one instruction about a window is an instruction to build one, and the ark's window is what makes the end of the Flood narrative possible — Noah opens it, sends out the raven and the dove, and learns that the waters are abated. Take the window away and you take away the ark's only instrument of knowledge; a vessel that cannot be looked out of cannot be navigated, which is why the brother of Jared's first question at 2:19 is 'whither shall we steer'. The Jaredites get Noah's ark with its window removed and its door still shut, and everything that follows — the stones, the touch of the finger, the vision of the premortal Christ — is the compensation for a hole in the roof that Genesis granted and Ether refuses. The refusal is also the tell: it is only worth denying a window to a reader who expects one.

2:23.note: A negation is harder to catalogue than a borrowing, and the row is written on the grounds that the thing denied is a KJV singleton and that the vessel denying it is otherwise built to Genesis 6's specification (see the Genesis 7:16 row at 2:17). 'Windows' on its own occurs in 26 KJV verses and points nowhere; what points is that this vessel, at this moment, in a chapter that has just quoted Genesis 6:3 verbatim, is told it cannot have the one thing Genesis 6:16 tells an ark-builder to make. Confidence is 'high' rather than 'certain' because the argument is inferential throughout: no words are shared, and a reader who does not grant that the barges are being written against the ark will not grant the row either.
2:23.text: A window shalt thou make to the ark, and in a cubit shalt thou finish it above; and the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof; with lower, second, and third stories shalt thou make it.

provenance.other: “to give them light” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Exodus 13:21 and Nehemiah 9:12, and in both the light is given by a pillar of fire so that a travelling people may go by night. Exodus 13:21: 'by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night.' Nehemiah 9:12: 'in the night by a pillar of fire, to give them light in the way wherein they should go.' The Book of Mormon's clause is 'neither shall ye take fire with you, for ye shall not go by the light of fire' — the same three terms, fire, light, going, in the same relation, negated.
provenance.significance: The Jaredite journey has been built on the wilderness guidance since 2:5, where the Lord goes before them and stands in a cloud. Exodus 13:21-22 gives that guidance two forms, a cloud by day and a fire by night, and Ether has taken the first and is here explicitly refused the second. What is withheld is not merely a lamp but the Exodus's own night-time mode of travel: Israel could 'go by day and night' because it had a fire to go by, and the Jaredites are told they will not. The stones of Ether 3 are then a third thing, neither cloud nor fire — light without burning, which is what a sealed vessel requires and what neither Genesis nor Exodus supplies.
provenance.alternative: The practical reason for the prohibition is obvious — an open flame in a sealed hull — and the verse gives it no scriptural framing. The row claims that the wording is Exodus's, not that the text says so.

2:23.note: Three shared terms and no shared clause, so this is an argument from the arrangement rather than from volume: the KJV has a formula in which fire gives light so that a people may go, it uses it twice, and Ether 2:23 negates all three of its terms in order. It is kept at 'moderate' for that reason — 'light of fire' occurs in 0 KJV verses, so there is nothing here to count. What raises it above coincidence is the company it keeps: this is the second negated ark-or-exodus provision in one verse, alongside the window of Genesis 6:16, and both are refusals of a precedent the chapter has otherwise been following closely.
2:23.text: And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night:

provenance.other: “that I should do unto thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 10:51: 'And Jesus answered and said unto him, What wilt thou that I should do unto thee? The blind man said unto him, Lord, that I might receive my sight.' The Book of Mormon's 'What will ye that I should do' takes 'I should do' from Mark and the plural 'will ye' from the same pericope's other half, Mark 10:36 and Matthew 20:32; Matthew's form of the Bartimaeus question is 'What will ye that I shall do unto you' (20:32).
provenance.significance: This is the finding the chapter is worth reading for. The KJV asks 'What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?' twice, and on both occasions the answer is about sight: to Bartimaeus, who says 'that I might receive my sight', and — in the Matthean plural of 20:32-33 — to the two blind men, who say 'that our eyes may be opened'. Ether 2:23 puts that question to a man in the dark, and the Lord's own completion of it is 'that ye may have light in your vessels'. The question the Gospels reserve for the blind is asked here about a hold with no windows, and it is asked, at 2:25, a second time, with the same result Mark's asking has: the petitioner must name what he wants before he can be given it. Recover the context and the theological point of Mark 10:51 comes with it — Jesus does not presume on the need, he requires it to be spoken — which is exactly the pedagogy of Ether 3:2-5, where the brother of Jared must propose the sixteen stones himself.
provenance.alternative: The interrogative is a natural English construction and the Book of Mormon uses it elsewhere (Alma 18:14, 3 Nephi 28:4). What makes this occurrence more than the formula recurring, in the sense of ADJUDICATING §4's Mosiah 29:2 ruling, is the object: alone among the Book of Mormon's uses, this one is answered with sight.

2:23.note: Five words of a KJV singleton, and the strongest kind of coincidence a catalogue can hope for — a rare interrogative whose two Gospel occurrences both concern the giving of sight, imported into the one Book of Mormon episode about the absence of light. That the Book of Mormon's phrasing fuses Mark's 'I should do' with the plural of Matthew 20:32 is itself evidence of the pericope rather than of a single verse, which is why both are recorded as composite. The row is 'high' and not 'certain' because 'what will ye that I should do' is short and idiomatic enough to have been composed without a source; the rarity count is what argues otherwise. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his passages.
2:23.text: And Jesus answered and said unto him, What wilt thou that I should do unto thee? The blind man said unto him, Lord, that I might receive my sight.

provenance.other: “as a whale in the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 32:2: 'thou art like a young lion of the nations, and thou art as a whale in the seas: and thou camest forth with thy rivers, and troubledst the waters with thy feet.' The KJV's only other whales are Genesis 1:21 and Job 7:12, neither of which is a simile. Ether 2:24 reads 'ye shall be as a whale in the midst of the sea'.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one whale-simile is an insult. It is addressed to Pharaoh king of Egypt in a lamentation, and the point of it is that the monster thrashing in the waters will be hauled out in a net and left on the open field for the birds (Ezekiel 32:3-4). Ether 2:24 gives the same simile to the Jaredites as a promise — you will be as a whale, and I will bring you up again out of the depths — so that the figure of a doomed sea-beast becomes the figure of a vessel that submerges and surfaces. The unstated correspondence is drowning: Pharaoh is the KJV's drowned king, the Red Sea is his grave, and the Book of Mormon has already run its Exodus through that drowning at 1 Nephi 4:2. Here the Pharaoh-image is turned inside out and given to the people crossing.

2:24.note: Four words on a KJV singleton, in a verse where the machine's rarity stream was right for once (Ezekiel 32:2 scored 2.00 and led the verse). The link is secure on rarity; what it does not do is import Ezekiel's argument, and a reader may reasonably hold that 'as a whale in the midst of the sea' is simply the available English for a large thing in deep water. Against that, the KJV offers no other English for it: the noun occurs three times in the Bible and only here in a comparison.
2:24.text: Son of man, take up a lamentation for Pharaoh king of Egypt, and say unto him, Thou art like a young lion of the nations, and thou art as a whale in the seas: and thou camest forth with thy rivers, and troubledst the waters with thy feet, and fouledst their rivers.

provenance.other: “from the depths of the sea” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 68:22: 'The Lord said, I will bring again from Bashan, I will bring my people again from the depths of the sea.' “bring me up again” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 71:20: 'shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth.' Ether 2:24's 'I will bring you up again out of the depths of the sea' is the two singletons fused — Psalm 68:22's sea and its first-person divine promise, Psalm 71:20's 'up again'. “depths of the sea” alone occurs in 3 KJV verses (Psalm 68:22, Isaiah 51:10, Micah 7:19).
provenance.significance: Psalm 68:22 is the KJV's one sentence in which the Lord promises, in his own voice, to fetch his people back out of the depths of the sea; the psalm is a march-of-God psalm whose Lord 'went before' his people through the wilderness (68:7), which is what Ether 2:5 has him doing. Psalm 71:20 supplies the resurrection cadence — 'shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth' — and with it the sense the Book of Mormon needs: not rescue from a sea, but being raised out of it. The barges are going under. The Lord's answer is not that they will float but that they will be brought up, which is the promise of Psalm 71:20 with the earth exchanged for the sea, and it converts the crossing into a burial and a raising. Ether 6:6-7 will bear this out: the vessels are 'buried in the deep' and rise again.
provenance.alternative: Micah 7:19's 'cast all their sins into the depths of the sea' is the better-known KJV phrase and the wrong one — its motion is downward and final, and nothing is brought up.

2:24.note: Two KJV singletons fused in one clause, which is about as strong as a five-word borrowing gets. The Book of Mormon has 'out of' where Psalm 68:22 has 'from', which is the only departure. The row is 'high' rather than 'certain' because the fusion means neither source is reproduced whole, and because a writer with the Psalter's cadences could have arrived at the sentence without either verse — but 'bring … up again … depths of the sea' assembles two phrases each of which the KJV uses once, and the coincidence of both in one clause is not a cheap one.
2:24.text: The Lord said, I will bring again from Bashan, I will bring my people again from the depths of the sea:

provenance.other: “the floods came” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Matthew 7:25 and 7:27, which are the same sentence twice: 'And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house.' The triad rain-floods-winds occurs nowhere else in the KJV. Ether 2:24 has 'the winds have gone forth out of my mouth, and also the rains and the floods have I sent forth', and 2:25 repeats it as 'the waves of the sea, and the winds which have gone forth, and the floods which shall come'.
provenance.significance: The parable's point is the difference between two builders, and the storm is identical in both halves — the same rain, the same floods, the same winds beat on both houses, and only the foundation decides. Ether 2:24-25 takes the triad and adds the one thing Matthew withholds: the storm's author. 'The winds have gone forth out of my mouth, and also the rains and the floods have I sent forth.' In the parable the weather is simply weather; here the Lord claims it, and immediately offers to prepare the vessel against what he has himself sent. That turns a parable about prudent building into an account of a test that its examiner is running, which is a fair description of the whole Jaredite ocean crossing.
provenance.alternative: 'The floods' is a Psalter word as well (Psalm 18:4, Jonah 2:3), and the sea-storm vocabulary of Jonah 2:3 — 'all thy billows and thy waves passed over me' — is closer to the maritime setting than Matthew's inland storm is.

2:24.note: No clause is shared and the setting is wrong — Matthew's storm hits a house, Ether's hits a boat — so the row rests entirely on the triad, which the KJV assembles in one place. It is written because the Book of Mormon assembles it twice in two verses, and because the second assembly at 2:25 keeps Matthew's own verb for the floods ('which shall come' against 'the floods came') while the first uses a different one. Moderate: a reader who thinks rain, wind and flood are simply what a storm consists of will decline this, and that reader is not being unreasonable. The counter is that a sea-storm does not obviously need rain in it at all, and this one has rain because Matthew's does.
2:24.whyNot: Rain, floods and winds are the natural constituents of any storm and their co-occurrence may be a fact about weather rather than about the KJV. The catalogue's own standard elsewhere is that a shared list is evidence only when the list is arbitrary; this one is not fully arbitrary.
2:24.text: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.
